stories.imageAlt: A check from the Georgia Department of Corrections dated Aug. 19, 2026, for $170,000. The recipient, account number and signature are redacted with black boxes.
stories.body:
As Georgia plans for its first execution in two years, a trove of records provides us with new information — and raises new questions — about the state’s lethal injection process.

Before I joined ProPublica in 2021, I had spent a year writing about a Georgia prison physician named Carlo Musso , one of the rare doctors who’d openly talked about his role in lethal injections. After he stepped away from that work, I wanted to know who replaced him, so I filed open records requests for documents that would shed light on that.

The role Musso held is so controversial that more than a dozen states have made it illegal to disclose the names of those involved with lethal injections. Georgia is among them. The state has gone to great lengths to hide the details around how it carries out lethal injections.

Georgia wouldn’t release records I had requested, claiming that its secrecy law is needed to prevent those helping with its executions from getting harassed by opponents of the death penalty.

I ended up suing the state. A few years later, a panel of three judges sided with me , and the state released some of the documents.

What I received reveals new details — and revives old questions — about Georgia’s lethal injection process. Among the discoveries: Georgia has made payments of more than $1.1 million since the COVID-19 pandemic for at least one contractor to work with the Corrections Department on its lethal injection process. During that period, the state carried out just a single execution.

The records also show that Georgia is paying far more for lethal injection-related costs than it did in the past. The state’s Corrections Department has spent an average of over $150,000 a year on those costs over the past decade. That’s substantially more than what it agreed to pay in the years before 2017, the records show.

Secrecy laws like Georgia’s shield the public from awareness of the growing costs of pharmacists concocting drugs and the doctors administering the injections. Legal experts say those costs reflect the challenges that corrections officials face in finding help with carrying out lethal injections, which can subject prisoners to torturous levels of pain.

“You wouldn’t have to pay this much money if the lethal injection process was an acceptable one,” said Deborah Denno, a Fordham University law professor who is an expert on the death penalty. “The process itself is so problematic that a lot of money has to be paid.”

Even after releasing the records, the Georgia Department of Corrections declined to answer my questions about the rising costs and the secrecy around lethal injections. The state attorney general’s office, which has represented the department in the lawsuit I filed for the records, also declined to comment for this story. State officials previously said that the Lethal Injection Secrecy Act allows the Corrections Department to protect contractors who would otherwise “ find themselves at the center of a firestorm of hate mail and midnight callers .” They have repeatedly argued that, without the secrecy law in place, Georgia wouldn’t be able to carry out lethal injections.

The secrets of Georgia’s death penalty process could face scrutiny in the coming days. After a recent Georgia Supreme Court ruling, which removed a barrier that had paused executions, state officials recently scheduled an execution for Sept. 16 , which would be its first in two years.

For every new scheduled execution, a new set of questions about the people behind the injections is likely to emerge.

It wasn’t long after Georgia traded the electric chair for lethal injections in the early 2000s that the state ratcheted up its secrecy.

That’s when opponents of the death penalty increased pressure on pharmaceutical companies to stop selling lethal injection drugs to states that could be used for executions.

By the end of that decade, the advocates’ campaign started to work. The last U.S. factory to make a key ingredient for lethal injections stopped doing so. States across the country scrambled to find new sources of the drugs.

Georgia, for its part, purchased drugs from a wholesaler whose business operated out of the back room of a London driving school .

But that backfired. The Drug Enforcement Administration seized the state’s supply of lethal injection drugs in 2011. Soon after, the European Union — made up of countries that oppose the death penalty — effectively banned companies from selling drugs to states if they were going to use them for executions.

Faced with dire lethal injection drug shortages, states turned to a more secret and at times sketchier source of drugs.

As Georgia’s supply was set to expire in 2013, it became one of the first states to place an order with compounding pharmacists, who mix raw ingredients to make custom drugs for patients. Although compounding pharmacies have legitimate uses, they are minimally regulated and their costs can be exorbitant.

That avenue was ideal for states that couldn’t buy execution drugs from more scrutinized pharmaceutical companies. But medical experts say that scant oversight of the compounding pharmacies increased the odds of a drug not working as intended.

In a 2013 affidavit filed on behalf of a Georgia prisoner, one pharmacy expert wrote that “highly unpredictable, rapidly evolving and potentially painful and agonizing, not to mention life-threatening, reactions may ensue” as the result of a lethal injection drug made by a compounding pharmacist.

Right around that time, Georgia lawmakers passed the Lethal Injection Secrecy Act. State prosecutors soon defended it in court. “Once that compounding pharmacy’s identity is revealed, how will the Department of Corrections ever get another compounding pharmacy to sell to us?” an assistant state attorney general said in a 2013 court hearing . “How will we get a doctor knowing that he is going to be, or she is going to be, dragged into court?”

At that time, I was reporting on how Georgia’s new secrecy law could affect Warren Lee Hill, who had been scheduled to be killed with drugs obtained from a compounding pharmacy. Hill’s attorneys said that their inability to get information about the drugs could cause “ irreparable harm ” to their client — and that argument won Hill a lengthy reprieve. He died by lethal injection in 2015.

In recent years, Texas , Indiana , and Arizona have all spent six-figure sums to renew their drug supplies from confidential sources. Defense attorneys have also tried to learn more information about those involved with the lethal injection process. They had hoped extra records might help them protect their clients’ rights.

But in Georgia, none have been successful.

Other states likewise spend large amounts of taxpayer dollars on secret contractors involved in the lethal injection process. Oklahoma went from paying a doctor $300 per execution to $15,000 . And the American Civil Liberties Union discovered that the Federal Bureau of Prisons had spent millions on staffing needed to carry out executions.

When I first requested records about Georgia’s lethal injections, the Corrections Department withheld entire documents that had “identifying information” about those involved with the process.

I asked the department to comply with the Georgia Open Records Act by releasing the documents with redactions. It refused. With the help of an attorney, I sued the department.

Georgia Attorney General Chris Carr, who defended the Corrections Department, wrote in a court filing that releasing the records “would not serve the interest of the public.”

The names of the people involved with the lethal injection process were redacted from the records that Georgia ultimately released to me. But the records show more than just the spending. They show the lengths the state took to protect its contractors.

Read More

Georgia is on the hook for attorney’s fees for its contractors should they face certain kinds of legal challenges, the records show. That means that taxpayers could shoulder the costs of legal representation in “any non-judicial proceeding.” One such example could be if a licensing board threatened to punish medical providers for participating in the lethal injection process — a threat that’s happened in North Carolina .

The records also show that Georgia officials may have disregarded their own financial policies. The Corrections Department requires detailed purchase orders to be kept and logged in the state’s financial system. But all that the department’s lawyers could provide me were handwritten checks, plus a series of one-page documents containing scant information about what the state was paying for — documents that hardly resembled the invoice of an official agency.

I’ve asked the department to provide purchasing records that had more details to comply with its policy.

It couldn’t.

“There are no other records,” wrote a lawyer for the Corrections Department.

stories.title: The New Threat to Citizenship in U.S. Territories
stories.summary: The Trump administration is expanding its attack against birthright citizenship. The post The New Threat to Citizenship in U.S. Territories appeared first on Foreign Policy In Focus .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Shutterstock

The Trump administration and its supporters are preparing a major change in U.S. colonial practices by moving to restrict birthright citizenship in U.S. territories.

Since the Supreme Court reaffirmed in Trump v. Barbara that people born in the United States are citizens of the United States, as guaranteed by the Citizenship Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment to the Constitution, the Trump administration has been seeking an exception for the territories. Trying to evade the Barbara decision, the White House and its allies in Congress are making new legal maneuvers that would prevent people born in the territories from being U.S. citizens.

“The Barbara case leaves the door open for Congressional action on citizenship in the American territories,” Representative Morgan Griffith (R-VA) said in a statement in July. “Just like Congress possesses the power to grant the territories Constitutional rights in statute, we have the power to take them away in statute.”

Citizenship in the Territories

Today, nearly four million people live in the five permanently inhabited territories of the United States, which are Guam, Puerto Rico, American Samoa, the Northern Mariana Islands, and the U.S. Virgin Islands. The residents of all five territories live under U.S. jurisdiction, but they endure significant limits to their rights and freedoms, such as unequal rights and unequal representation in Congress. They have never been treated as equals, especially as it concerns citizenship.

Under current U.S. colonial practices , birthright citizenship in the territories is determined by Congress, not the constitution. Whereas people born in the states can claim citizenship under the Citizenship Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment , people born in the territories depend on legislation passed by Congress, which does not legislate equally across the territories.

Congress has granted birthright citizenship to four of the five territories, leaving the exception of American Samoa , whose residents are classified as U.S. nationals. Several American Samoans who live in Alaska are now being persecuted due to their separate legal status and confusion over its meaning.

Although most people born in the territories are U.S. citizens, the matter of who can claim birthright citizenship in the territories remains contested.

U.S. officials have largely operated on the principle that Congress decides whether people living in the territories are U.S. citizens. Multiple U.S. administrations have taken the position that the Citizenship Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment does not apply to the territories, despite its guarantee of citizenship to anyone born “in the United States” and “subject to the jurisdiction thereof.”

U.S. officials have often rooted their arguments in the Insular Cases , a notorious set of Supreme Court rulings from the early twentieth century that established a legal foundation for U.S. colonialism. Although critics have spent decades criticizing the Insular Cases for their racist arguments that rationalize a doctrine of separate and unequal for people living in the territories, multiple U.S. administrations have embraced them, relying on them to keep the territories under U.S. control.

“The Supreme Court determined that the unincorporated territories do not form part of ‘the United States’ within the meaning of the Constitution,” a think tank founded by former Vice President Mike Pence noted in a recent report.

U.S. leaders continue to rely on the Insular Cases, but critics insist that they are unconstitutional and that the Citizenship Clause covers the territories. Initially, “the long-settled understanding of the Citizenship Clause was that it applied equally to people born in the states and territories alike,” Neil Weare, co-director of Right to Democracy, explained in SCOTUSblog earlier this year.

Although the Supreme Court has largely avoided the issue, some conservative and liberal justices have displayed growing skepticism of the Insular Cases. During a case in 2022, Justices Neil Gorsuch and Sonia Sotomayor issued strong criticisms, even signaling that it is time to overrule them.

“The Insular Cases have no foundation in the Constitution and rest instead on racial stereotypes,” Gorsuch wrote . “They deserve no place in our law.” Sotomayor agreed, writing that “those cases were premised on beliefs both odious and wrong.”

When the Supreme Court had an opportunity to take up the matter in a petition involving John Fitisemanu , an American Samoan living in the United States who sought citizenship under the Fourteenth Amendment and an end to the Insular Cases, it declined to consider the issue, however.

The New Threat

As U.S. colonial practices have come under scrutiny, most U.S. leaders have responded by making new commitments to empire. Not only has the Trump administration been trying to seize other countries and territories, but it has been moving to restrict the rights and freedoms of people living in the territories already under U.S. control.

After the Supreme Court reaffirmed birthright citizenship in Trump v. Barbara , Vice President JD Vance said on Fox News that “it’s a great idea” to impose new restrictions on citizenship in the territories.

“We’re certainly looking at that,” Vance said .

Not long after Vance acknowledged the administration’s interests, Representative Griffith introduced new legislation into Congress that would end birthright citizenship in the territories. Griffith called his legislation the “ End Birthright Citizenship for Territories Act .”

In a statement, Griffith said that his goal is to end what he called “birth tourism,” but his legislation would end birthright citizenship for anyone born in the territories starting on January 1, 2027.

“The bill would strip automatic U.S. citizenship from children born in Puerto Rico, Guam, the U.S. Virgin Islands, and the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands beginning in 2027,” Representative Stacey Plaskett (D-VI) explained in a statement. “Its sweeping language could leave children born in the U.S. territories citizens of nowhere.”

Still, the Trump administration saw an opening. On August 6, the president issued two new executive orders to limit birthright citizenship in the United States, adding new language about the territories, something he had not included in his order that was struck down by the Supreme Court.

The new language “suggests and perhaps even invites Congress to move ahead with legislation such as the ‘End Birthright Citizenship For Territories Act,’” Weare warned in a press release.

Resistance and Empire

Recent moves to end birthright citizenship in the territories do not necessarily have any traction in Congress. For instance, Representative Kimberlyn King-Hinds, a Republican from the Northern Mariana Islands, has insisted that Griffith’s legislation “will not become law.” Nevertheless, these efforts by the Trump administration are having significant consequences, perhaps some that it had not anticipated.

One is that anticolonial movements are responding with a new sense of urgency. At Right to Democracy , the organization co-founded by Weare, lawyers and activists are organizing resistance. They are issuing press releases that call attention to the Trump administration’s actions. They are also promoting an informational page that explains the issues at stake, including the colonial history of birthright citizenship in the territories.

Journalists are also providing critical coverage. Newspapers in territories that have been granted birthright citizenship by Congress, including Guam , Puerto Rico , the Northern Mariana Islands , and the U.S. Virgin Islands , are all reporting on the issue. Newspapers in American Samoa are also filing reports, publishing press releases from Right to Democracy.

At the same time, however, the Trump administration and its allies in Congress remain determined to move against birthright citizenship in the territories. Rather than acting in ways that reflect the ideals of freedom and equality that they claimed to support during their celebrations of the two-hundred-and-fiftieth anniversary of U.S. independence, they are working to strengthen the forces of empire and colonialism. Trump has even begun openly bragging about empire, shattering the longstanding norm of empire denial.

What the Trump administration and its supporters are doing, in short, is preparing for a new era of U.S. colonialism in which people in the territories live less like citizens and more like subjects, just as King George III had wanted for people living in the British colonies at the time of the American Revolution. The new colonial push threatens to impose greater hardships on the people of the territories, whose rights and freedoms have always been vulnerable to manipulation by Washington.

“The people of U.S. territories are subject to novel social and economic experiments without their say or consent,” Weare wrote in SCOTUSblog. “None of this can be squared with the principles of ‘consent of the governed’ and all ‘created equal’ on which the United States was founded 250 years ago.”

stories.title: Trump Can Escalate the Iran War But He Still Has No Clear Endgame
stories.summary: Seven months into the conflict, Washington can still destroy targets. What it has not shown is how the war ends. The post Trump Can Escalate the Iran War But He Still Has No Clear Endgame appeared first on Foreign Policy In Focus .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Shutterstock

On September 3, Vice President JD Vance said that the confrontation with Iran was not really a war and declined to say when it might end. A day later, President Donald Trump called the conflict “small potatoes.” By then, the fighting had entered its seventh month, cost the United States more than $37.5 billion, and killed 18 U.S. service members. The language has shifted. The strategic problem has not.

The most revealing feature of Trump’s Iran war is no longer the scale of the military campaign. It is the gap between what American force can destroy and what Washington has been able to achieve politically. The United States and Israel have inflicted severe damage on Iran’s military infrastructure, yet there is still no durable settlement, no agreed nuclear framework, and no clear answer to the most basic question of strategy: what would victory actually look like?

Trump initially presented the conflict as something that could end quickly. Six months later, he posted “MISSION ACCOMPLISHED 2026” even as negotiations stalled, sanctions intensified, and intermittent strikes continued. Washington has shifted from sustained bombing toward economic pressure, naval enforcement, and renewed attacks around the Strait of Hormuz. That is a change in method, not an end state.

A military operation is not a strategy. Bombing can destroy infrastructure, weaken military capabilities, or create temporary deterrence. It cannot by itself answer the political questions that follow. What concessions from Tehran would count as success? Is the objective a nuclear agreement, limits on missiles, freedom of navigation through Hormuz, a different regional balance, political transformation inside Iran, or some combination of these? And under what conditions would the United States stop fighting?

Those questions have become harder to answer because the administration’s public objectives have multiplied. Nuclear proliferation, Iranian military power, regional security, Hormuz, and political change have all appeared at different points. When objectives accumulate without a clear hierarchy, escalation can begin to substitute for strategy.

The real test of American power is not whether Washington can inflict more damage. It is whether it can shape the political trajectory of the conflict. Iran has absorbed enormous losses and still retained enough asymmetric capacity to impose costs around Hormuz. Gulf governments, meanwhile, are increasingly hedging against the uncertainty created by the conflict. Rather than producing a more stable regional order, the war has created new doubts for the very partners American power is supposed to reassure.

That leads to another problem: alliance management. A powerful state does not merely join coalitions; it sets priorities and decides which allied preferences serve its own interests. A Stimson Center study argues that the Iran war shows important features of alliance entanglement and that U.S. core security interests alone do not fully explain the decision to enter the conflict. One need not accept every part of that argument to see the danger. Alliances should expand American options not make disengagement politically harder or turn a partner’s preferred objective into an automatic U.S. commitment.

Congress has already signaled its concern. In June, the House passed a War Powers resolution directing the president to remove U.S. forces from hostilities with Iran, and the Senate approved the same measure later that month. Whatever the continuing dispute over presidential authority, the votes mattered politically: both chambers challenged a conflict whose legal basis and endgame remained contested.

The argument is also moving through Trump’s own coalition. MAGA is not a unified antiwar movement, and many Republican voters initially backed the campaign. But the war has exposed a genuine dispute over what “America First” means. Noninterventionist voices such as Tucker Carlson have accused the administration of reproducing the Middle Eastern wars Trump once condemned, while hawks have attacked the idea of ending the conflict without maximal concessions from Tehran. Trump is being pulled between two definitions of strength.

That contradiction matters because his political rise depended partly on rejecting the foreign-policy establishment’s record of long wars with unclear exits. If “America First” comes to mean prolonged deployments, rising energy costs, recurring escalation, and open-ended commitments in the Middle East, Trump risks recreating the very model he used to discredit Washington’s strategic class.

Public opinion is making the problem harder to ignore. A Reuters/Ipsos poll released on September 4 found that only 25 percent of Americans believe that the Iran war is worthwhile. Polls do not determine strategy, but they raise the political cost of a war whose objective remains difficult to define.

The longer a conflict continues without a decisive political result, the harder it becomes to leave. The harder it becomes to leave, the greater the temptation to escalate so that earlier sacrifices do not appear wasted. Policymakers can then end up continuing a war not because its original goals are becoming more attainable but because ending it would expose how little those costs achieved.

This is the central danger of Trump’s Iran war. The administration entered the conflict promising strength. But military strength without strategic discipline can become a liability. A superpower that can destroy targets but cannot define an acceptable settlement, manage allied ambitions, reassure regional partners, or specify the conditions for disengagement is exercising military power without fully exercising strategic power.

The crisis, then, is not simply that Trump went to war with Iran. It is that months of fighting have exposed the absence of a coherent regional strategy capable of turning American military superiority into a durable political outcome. Until Washington closes that gap, it risks fighting harder not because it knows what victory requires but because it does not know how to stop.

That is not strategic strength. It is strategic drift.

stories.title: Ken Paxton’s Financial Disclosures Appear to Violate Federal Ethics Law, Experts Say
stories.summary: The post Ken Paxton’s Financial Disclosures Appear to Violate Federal Ethics Law, Experts Say appeared first on ProPublica .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.imageAlt: A close-up screenshot of an amended financial disclosure form highlighting a joint asset listed as undeveloped land in Johnson County, Texas, valued between $15,001 and $50,000.
stories.body:
The Republican U.S. Senate nominee from Texas appears to have omitted rental income and multiple mortgages from his recent financial disclosures, making it difficult for voters to get the full picture of his wealth.

Co-published with The Texas Tribune

Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton appears to have violated federal ethics law in significant ways when filing recent disclosures of his assets and liabilities, creating confusion about his net worth and holdings, a review by ProPublica and The Texas Tribune found.

Among them: Paxton, the Republican nominee for U.S. Senate, reported owning seven homes but said he earned no income from any. Yet all but one was listed for rent during the reporting periods, and some current residents and neighbors at those addresses confirmed that the properties were rented, the news organizations found. Receiving income and not reporting it is a violation of federal disclosure law, three ethics experts said.

Additionally, Paxton did not disclose mortgages for three condos at a Utah golf resort that federal law requires him to list as liabilities if they are not personal residences.

He also valued his stake in a vacant plot of Texas land at up to $50,000 on last year’s filing, but his business partner told the newsrooms Paxton’s share for years has been worth about $1 million. Federal financial disclosure law requires property to be listed at fair market value.

The apparent errors and omissions the newsrooms found obscure the extent of Paxton’s income streams, assets and debt, making it difficult for voters to make sense of his finances as they mull whether to support him in November’s election, the ethics experts said.

“It reflects either pure sloppiness on Paxton’s part or a deliberate effort to conceal some of his investments and property holdings,” said Craig Holman, a government affairs lobbyist for the nonpartisan good-government group Public Citizen.

If Paxton wins, an incomplete picture of his finances could prevent watchdogs from evaluating his conflicts of interest as a senator, Holman and others said.

The apparent omissions are part of a pattern for Paxton. Over three terms as attorney general, he has withheld financial information that could explain how he became a multimillionaire and had the resources to purchase more than a dozen properties in five states. He began including many of these on his state disclosures only after the Texas Ethics Commission closed a loophole in 2024 that Paxton had cited to leave them off. Most were acquired while Paxton earned a government salary of $153,750.

In the new federal disclosure, filed in August after Paxton received a three-month extension, he reported a net worth between $1 million and $27 million. That is a significantly higher range than the negative $1.9 million to $11.1 million net worth he reported a year ago, before he had secured the Republican nomination but after he had declared his candidacy for federal office.

The spike was driven not by Paxton’s acquisition of more assets but because the reported value on several of his properties soared.

Paxton’s report omitted listing as assets seven properties worth about $5.2 million collectively, including the Utah condos for which he did not disclose mortgages. He co-owns all of his known real estate holdings with his estranged wife, state Sen. Angela Paxton, property records show. The eight he reported are held by their blind trust, which is managed by a family friend.

Federal rules do not require candidates to report as assets personal homes or properties from which they don’t earn money, even if the properties are worth millions.

At a time when voters feel anxious about their own personal finances and dislike the idea of politicians getting rich in office, it would be wise for Paxton to be more transparent about his wealth, said Texas ethics and campaign finance lawyer Andrew Cates.

“If it were me trying to get people’s vote, I would err on the side of transparency rather than not,” Cates said.

Paxton declined to be interviewed and did not answer detailed questions about how he filled out the disclosure forms. Madison Cercy, a spokesperson for his campaign, said Paxton “has had a long and successful career outside of public service, including running his own small business as a lawyer. Stirring up partisan allegations is nothing more than a bad attempt to manufacture controversy where none exists.”

Before being elected to the state Legislature in 2002, Paxton worked at a law firm in the Dallas area and was a corporate attorney for JCPenney. His state financial disclosure for 2001 listed assets totaling no more than $170,000, a ProPublica and Tribune analysis found.

By 2015, his household net worth had grown to $5.4 million, according to financial records lawmakers subpoenaed in 2023 after impeaching Paxton on charges that he took bribes in exchange for helping an Austin real estate investor.

The records, few of which were admitted into evidence during the 10-day Senate trial that resulted in his acquittal, document how Paxton built a diverse portfolio that included investments in a cellphone tower , an HVAC company, a cement supplier and a police body camera manufacturer. He netted $2.2 million when Motorola acquired the body camera firm in 2019 , according to his income tax return from that year.

Shortly after, he went on a real estate buying spree, snapping up six properties in Oklahoma, Florida, Utah and Hawaii. His impeachment defense team said Paxton made a prudent shift toward real estate at a time of rock-bottom interest rates.

Questions about Paxton’s integrity have dogged him in the race for U.S. Senate. His opponent, Democratic state Rep. James Talarico, entered September with a narrow polling lead — uncharted territory in a state where Republicans have not lost a statewide race in 32 years.

A University of Texas/Texas Politics Project poll released last week found that just a third of respondents viewed Paxton as “honest and trustworthy.” The same day the statewide poll was published, a super PAC supporting Talarico hit the airwaves with an ad that labeled the attorney general as “the most corrupt politician in Texas.” The commercial included a reference to Paxton’s recently disclosed net worth.

Talarico’s net worth, according to his most recent personal financial disclosure, was between $67,000 and $305,000. The range changed little from the previous year. Like Paxton, Talarico did not include his single personal residence among his reported assets.

James Henson, director of the Texas Politics Project, said the questions surrounding Paxton’s latest financial disclosures reinforce a longstanding narrative that the attorney general is secretive about his finances and may have leveraged his public position for personal gain.

“It’s his choice how much he explains or doesn’t explain,” Henson said. “But I think that comes with a potential cost, and we’re seeing that in public opinion.”

Paxton’s pivot to real estate appears to be a way to supplement his salary as attorney general. The newsrooms found recent rental listings for six of the properties he disclosed but for which he said he derived no income: two homes in Ocala, Florida; a home and a condo in Austin; a home in College Station, Texas; and a vacation lodge in Broken Bow, Oklahoma.

A tenant confirmed to the newsrooms she’s living at one of Florida houses. At the Austin condo complex, a next-door neighbor said Paxton’s unit has a renter. And the five-bedroom, three-story Oklahoma lodge he owns is listed online as a short-term rental for up to $1,200 a night, with fall bookings filling up fast.

On his disclosure forms, which require real estate income to be reported, Paxton for each property selected the option “None (or less than $201).”

Federal law requires candidates who aren’t currently in Congress to report all loans exceeding $10,000, except those for personal residences. Paxton did not report three mortgages totaling $1.3 million for condos at the Black Desert Resort in southwest Utah, renowned for its world-class golf course. He purchased the properties in February; the reporting period for the most recent disclosure ran through mid-May.

Reporters found the mortgage documents in local land records. Each contains an addendum to the mortgage that is used for rental properties, said New Jersey real estate lawyer Daniel M. Shlufman. That addendum removes a requirement that the unit be owner-occupied and allows the lender to collect rent directly from tenants if Paxton were to default on the loan.

Paxton purchased another condo at the resort in 2025, which he disclosed on his most recent report as an asset and a liability. The land records show he obtained a $640,000 mortgage for it. The resort advertises a program in which it leases units purchased by investors, but it declined to say if Paxton’s properties were enrolled in it.

“It’s kind of mind-boggling to think about having four homes at one resort property and imagining those are for personal use,” said Cynthia Brown, a senior lawyer at the government watchdog Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington.

The most significant changes between Paxton’s 2025 and 2026 reports were the valuations of the Oklahoma lodge and a plot of land outside of Fort Worth, whose value he said had increased by millions of dollars.

He appears to have switched from reporting the properties’ assessed values, which are set by the local county, to the loftier estimates of what they would fetch on the open market.

Paxton’s initial use of the lowball values appears to defy federal rules aimed at bringing candidates’ disclosed property values in line with what they’re actually worth. While the Senate Ethics Committee instructs filers that they can use a recent tax assessment to set the worth of certain property, they must adjust it to market value if it is assessed below that. In these cases, valuations must be disclosed as a specific dollar figure rather than a range.

On both his annual reports as a Senate candidate, Paxton listed ranges for the value of each property he disclosed.

Last year, Paxton reported the Oklahoma lodge, just north of the Texas border, as worth between $100,001 and $250,000. The local county assesses the property at $176,000. Its estimated market value, meanwhile, is more than $1.5 million, according to real estate websites. This year, Paxton’s disclosure valued the property at between $1 million and $5 million.

Likewise, Paxton valued a 42-acre plot of undeveloped land in Johnson County, south of Fort Worth, at between $15,001 and $50,000 last year. The county assesses the property as farmland worth $20,008, but estimates its market value is $2.9 million. This year, Paxton’s disclosure said the property was worth between $1 million and $5 million.

Paxton bought the property in 2006 with a group of investors including Rob Orr, with whom he served in the Texas House of Representatives. Orr, who manages the investment, said in an interview that Paxton’s 20% stake is worth about $1 million.

“It would have been around a million for quite a while, probably the last four or five years,” Orr said. “It has increased in value because of zoning and because of time.”

The group bought the plot to hold onto, Orr said, until creeping growth from the Dallas-Fort Worth area made it attractive for redevelopment. He said the group is negotiating a sale to a developer. Last year, Orr persuaded the City Council in Burleson to rezone the land, which had been restricted to agriculture, to permit retail and housing.

Read More

Paxton’s move to significantly revalue his assets without explaining why is “very strange,” said Margaret Dylus-Yukins, senior counsel for ethics at the nonpartisan Campaign Legal Center, which advocates for strong disclosure rules. Dylus-Yukins, who worked for six years analyzing executive branch officials’ financial disclosures for the U.S. Office of Government Ethics, said the agency would ask filers to explain major changes in writing.

“When you have public officials that appear to be fudging the numbers on their disclosure forms, and the Senate Ethics Committee is letting that slide, then you’re not only eroding trust in the committee but the candidate himself,” Dylus-Yukins said, referring to the significant differences between the filings.

The ethics committee did not respond to requests for comment. Candidates or senators who willingly falsify financial disclosures can be fined up to $50,000 or prosecuted for making a false statement to the government, a felony. The committee rarely investigates senators and has not formally sanctioned a member in 19 years .

Candidates do not have to file any more federal financial disclosures before the November election.

stories.title: Your Perception Of Time Is, In Fact, Warped
stories.summary: The post Your Perception Of Time Is, In Fact, Warped appeared first on NOEMA .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
We keep marveling at how fast the years go by. The deeper problem is that we’re forgetting them — and losing the quiet, boring moments where memory forms.

Mike Mariani is a writer and journalist based in the D.C. area, and the author of “What Doesn’t Kill Us Makes Us,” published in August 2022 by Penguin Random House

We’ve long been ensorcelled by the passage of time. Puckered leaves fluttering from the spidery arms of barren trees. Grains of sand tumbling through the delicate neck of an hourglass. A curved cornice perched over a snow-covered mountain, awaiting an avalanche to bring it down. These evocative emblems of seasons, hours, and the vicissitudes they leave in their wake speak to the bittersweet relationship we’ve cultivated with this unit of measurement.

Whether in Proustian reveries, digital photo libraries, or the watchful doppelgänger that gazes out at us each morning, ever-so-slightly altered, we’re inclined to a tender wistfulness toward time — the persistent awareness that, however fast or slow, it’s forever slipping through our fingers.

But lately, our relationship to the months, years and decades that landscape our lives has shifted in some unsettling ways. Instead of regarding the passage of time with introspection or melancholy, many of us now observe it with a mounting sense of alarm.

You don’t have to look very far to find ample evidence that we are experiencing a metaphysical crack-up around time. There’s a growing conviction among people from all walks of life that time is moving faster than it did several decades ago — or even prior to the Covid pandemic. While this belief crept into the zeitgeist like a sly, slinking fog, the refrains are now so pervasive that they’ve started to supplant idle chatter on the weather. Our focus has shifted from rejoicing in cloudless days or grousing over gloomy skies to fixating on the dizzying speed at which our lives are hurtling by.

This is particularly evident on sites like Reddit, where users now regularly commiserate over how rapidly the years are passing. A farmer whose work cycles alongside the seasons “can’t believe how fast this year has gone.” A middle school teacher recounts how she finds herself “having these conversations with students … who are perturbed by the speed of life.” Perhaps most tellingly, for a programmer, the “pandemic years blurred together, and everything after feels compressed, like one long season instead of separate years.” Civilizational events, including not only Covid but also climate change, large-scale armed conflict and the rise of AI “have piled up so quickly that it feels like we’re living through multiple decades at once.”

In recent years, these stray observations have coalesced into a chorus. Everyone from Boomers to Zoomers is mystified at how the passage of time has sped up, and feels disoriented by the strange velocity that’s colored how we’re living through the 2020s. But to hear these stifled laments is also to observe the absurdity of contemporary American life: While so many of us agree that our relationship to time has been warped, our collective response has been to shake it off and move on. It’s as though we all started losing our depth perception at the same time — crashing into road medians, pratfalling down staircases — and instead of resolving to rectify the predicament, we’ve simply resigned ourselves to daily collisions and collapses.

In some ways, the scale of this phenomenon resembles an episode of mass cognitive dissonance, or even a population-level folie à deux. It’s worth asking if something about our internal mechanisms for gauging the passage of time has changed — or been irrevocably thrown out of sync with human timekeeping and the atomic clocks we’ve structured civilization around for nearly a century. Or, alternatively, perhaps the pandemic spoiled our capacity to judge duration, expanding and contracting our sense of time over and over until the fabric grew loose and rippled, an undifferentiated mass of fibers stretched into a form we no longer recognize.

A Theory Of Relativity

Scientists and academics have been grappling with some of these questions since the 19th century. In the 1890s, renowned French philosopher Paul Janet proposed that human beings experience time in proportion to their age. When we’re 10 years old, one year is fully 10% of our entire lifetimes; as a result, we process it with slow, substantive vividness. When we’re 50 years old, on the other hand, that same year represents only 2% of our lives, and we experience it with corresponding ephemerality and diminished gravitas. Janet’s theory would come to be known as “logarithmic time perception,” a reference to the measurement scale that represents mathematical figures proportionately (it’s sometimes referred to as the “time alive” theory).

William James picked up where Janet left off, positing in “Principles of Psychology” that time moves more slowly for young people, who slingshot themselves into fresh experiences every day. “Apprehension is vivid, retentiveness strong, and our recollections of that time, like those of a time spent in rapid and interesting travel, are of something intricate, multitudinous, and long-drawn-out,” he writes.

“You don’t have to look very far to find ample evidence that we are experiencing a metaphysical crack-up around time.”

James argues that the absorbing episodes children and teenagers so often find themselves in give the brain more to chew on — both in the moment and long after the moment’s passed. Because their exploits are consistently novel and stimulating, young people have the retrospective sensation that those specific intervals of time were fuller, deeper, more robust.

As we grow older, however, we become more immersed in patterns and routines, without the same opportunities to process new information, foster fresh skills or feel our way through unfamiliar circumstances that galvanize our intellects. We’re living by rote, so to speak, and our consciousness slides into a more dulled, dampened state. As a result, James notes, “the days and the weeks smooth themselves out in recollection to contentless units, and the years grow hollow and collapse.”

Though James was writing before the fields of neuroscience and psychology were even established — Freud had yet to publish his first book — his insights have been embraced by researchers more than a century later. Many of them now argue that the way we gauge time is inextricably linked to how active and engaged our brains are, and the extent to which we form memories.

When we’re seeing, hearing, touching and tasting exotic sights, sounds, surfaces and foods that arouse our senses, we’re far more likely to lay down new memories. Those recollections inform how we retrospectively evaluate the passage of time, giving it that languorous, “long-drawn-out” quality James described. “We only remember things which are novel or exciting or scary or have some visceral meaning to them,” Luke Jones, a psychologist at the University of Manchester, explained to me. “And your retrospective perception of duration is based on memory.”

But while we’ve long established that humans perceive time in an elastic, subjective way, that knowledge could not have prepared us for the Covid pandemic. That generational event bowed and buckled the way so many of us experience those hourglasses and cornices, swapping out placid reflection for consternation and dread. Over three years of lockdowns, quarantines and the claustrophobic monotony they inspired, countless Americans told anyone who would listen how different time felt to them. The weeks and months, we stammered, felt “stretched,” “warped,” “blurred.”

In 2023, researchers at Baylor University set out to legitimize these anecdotes. A team of sociologists published a study using Gallup data collected at the height of the pandemic to analyze how people perceived time during the period. The authors found that Americans experienced “time disorientation” in multiple directions, with time speeding up, slowing down and days blending together to the point of indistinguishability.

Another study of Uruguayan university students, published in “Time & Society” in 2022, found that 80% of students surveyed felt time had either sped up or slowed down during the pandemic. These findings were replicated in other parts of the world, including Argentina and Iraq . The co-authors of the “Time & Society” paper also noted an intriguing irony: In instances where excessive free time caused by lockdowns or other public health measures led to boredom, “time would be slow in the moment, but looking back on the experience retrospectively, people would feel that time flew.”

This points to a crucial aspect of time perception, one that continues to captivate me: We gauge the speed of time based on one set of factors in the moment — how engaged or stimulated we are — while using a distinct set of criteria to evaluate it retrospectively (the degree to which we formed memories). People trapped in their homes during the pandemic with little to do suffered a worst-case scenario, temporally speaking: the emptiness of their days slowed them to a crawl, while the insipid repetition of their experiences yielded few memories, causing wide swaths of time to, as James puts it, “grow hollow and collapse.”

When I spoke to Marc Wittmann, one of the 2022 study’s co-authors and a time perception researcher at the Institute for Frontier Areas in Psychology and Mental Health in Germany, he explained that the lack of distinct markers during the pandemic made each day look exactly alike, contributing to time disorientation. “Every day was the same,” he said. “Monday used to be the day you went skating, Tuesday was the day you spent with your friends. We used to have something associated with each day.” But all of this disappeared during global lockdowns, he said. Wittmann calls this “Blursday.”

“We’re living by rote, so to speak, and our consciousness slides into a more dulled, dampened state.”

The surge in time disorientation so many of us experienced during the pandemic came to be known as the “2020 effect.” The abrupt upheaval and subsequent tedium of restrictive, repetitive routines in those years led to the sensation of days bleeding into each other, time “stretching” and people losing the ability to recall events sequentially — as though our memories were shuffled and rearranged during a game of three-card monte.

But the most relevant question in 2026 isn’t whether the pandemic influenced how we experience time. A raft of academic papers demonstrate that it clearly did. The question now is whether our perception of time ever snapped back to the way it was before that generational event.

The Internal Clock Fallacy

To determine why our internal clocks sped up over the past few years, it helps to understand exactly what we mean by “internal clocks.” For years, time perception researchers have been trying to explain how human beings subjectively gauge duration. But it’s proven to be a stubborn riddle. One reason for this is that we have no organ or system dedicated to sensing time. Instead, as one 2016 paper puts it , “Psychological time is an abstraction, a construct or epiphenomenon of our mind’s functioning that we create in order to explain the coherence of events.”

Nevertheless, researchers were convinced for years that humans possessed a specific mechanism for measuring time — a theory referred to as the “internal clock model.” Though the model served as a convenient explanation for how humans tell time, scientists eventually grew skeptical of it. “Back then, there was a very anthropocentric model that was suspiciously similar to actual man-made clocks,” said Dean Buonomano, a neuroscientist at the University of California, Los Angeles. “You have some oscillator ticking away at some frequency, and then counting the time units, much like clocks work.” Another problem with the internal clock model was that scientists struggled to find hard evidence for its existence. As Warrick Roseboom, a psychologist at the University of Sussex, told me, “Researchers were just like, ‘Oh, you have a clock in your brain. We just need to find where the clock in your brain is.’”

But scientists never found the clock, and for some the model lost its credibility. Meanwhile, Roseboom and other academics began exploring alternative theories. In 2022, he and several colleagues at the University of Sussex published the results of a study that showed participants short videos to determine whether there was a relationship between the way we process the world around us and how we gauge the passage of time.

In the experiment, the amount of activity the videos elicited in participants’ brains was strongly correlated with their subjective sense of how much time passed. When the participants detected more happening in the videos, it triggered large changes in brain activity associated with visual processing, creating the sensation that more time had gone by. Roseboom and his co-authors concluded that we tell time based on “the accumulation of salient changes in the perceptual processing hierarchy” — or, as co-author Maxine Sherman said when the paper was published, “the brain just ‘counts’ how much ‘stuff’ has happened, which is very intuitive.”

One of the paper’s key takeaways is that our perception of time isn’t based on any fixed sense of duration. We do not, in fact, have an internal clock measuring minutes, hours and days. Instead, we use our external environment as a proxy for the passage of time. The more “stuff” our sensory cortex is picking up on, the more time we register as passing.

This new way of looking at time perception could shed light on why so many people feel like time is speeding up today. We’re inundated with videos, images, notifications and a cavalcade of content 24 hours a day, forcing our brains to contend with far more information than they needed to 10 or 20 years ago. Read Noema in print.

When I reached out to James Hyman, a neuroscientist at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas, he felt that applying Roseboom and his co-authors’ new theory of time perception to our current media ecosystem explained why so many people now feel flummoxed by the speed of their lives. “We’re constantly moving onto the next thing,” he said. “And the more things that we experience that cause us to move forward, well, if our brains are only able to tell time by counting things, then we’re jamming lots more things in there.” When we’re flooded with text, images and glowing blue light, our brains are tricked into speeding up the internal proxy mechanisms they use for measuring time. As a result, time feels like it’s moving faster and faster.

“We have no organ or system dedicated to sensing time.”

But the casino-like frenzy of our digital environments is only part of the reason our perception of time is changing. Remember that we assess duration from multiple vantage points, including retrospectively, when we gauge how much time we feel passed during a specific period. When we tell our spouse that “this week flew by,” we’re engaging in retrospective time perception. Arguably the most important variable in those judgments is memory — whether we formed them, how many we formed, how vivid they are.

Memories are the trees, shrubs and undulating peaks that landscape our past, preventing it from hollowing out and collapsing in on itself. (Smooth and featureless as the interior of a spaceship, the pandemic had no landscape, and our memory of it collapsed accordingly.) Because of this variability, retrospective time perception is even more subjective than other forms of time judgment, given its outsized dependence on “things which are novel or exciting or scary or have some visceral meaning to them.” The memories that stem from those stimuli are our footprints in the snow, giving our past the solidity and verisimilitude that would otherwise blow away in the past’s enveloping whiteout.

Our memories are the key to the central irony of our supersaturated world. Roseboom’s theory posits that time spent in an environment overflowing with visual information should feel long and robust. “You would think that because we’re paying more attention to more things, that retrospectively time should feel longer,” Jones noted. “But I think we’ve got the worst of all worlds.” Because while we encounter a glittering constellation of apps, games and videos beckoning us at every turn, eager to light up our sensory cortex, they’re not generating the indelible experiences crucial to forming memories. “When you get to the end of the day, you look back and there’s no meaningful content there. It’s just the same blur, the same stuff, and there’s nothing distinctive about it.”

Wittmann agrees that toggling between apps on our phone and numbing ourselves with Instagram reels can impoverish our retrospective perception of time. “When we’re on digital media, time passes very quickly,” he explained. “You lose yourself. You’re jumping around like mad in these apps, and you can’t put them into memory and later recall them, because the experiences just vanish.”

Browsing, scrolling and swiping are more likely to quiet or even anesthetize our brains than activate them in the ways required to form memories. As a result, spending an hour on TikTok might feel like 10 or 15 minutes, because we don’t have any of the “intricate, multitudinous, and long-drawn-out” sensations that give time depth and fullness. Instead, it all blends together in a turbulent vortex, overwhelming the senses rather than engaging them on the level necessary to endure over time. It’s easy to extrapolate this further and speculate how spending several hours a day on social media distorts our sense of time, giving us the impression that we were awake for just 12 or 13 hours of the day. Over months and years, surrendering this much time to our ersatz digital warrens can lead to a sense of deprivation — a feeling that years have been carved out of our lives.

According to Wittmann and other researchers, social media platforms are uniquely effective at short-circuiting our retrospective time perception. After spending time on these apps, the abstract field our mind’s eye draws from to make sense of recent experiences is left barren, devoid of the evocative wisps we integrate into the hazy memory palace that ultimately serves as our past. Instead, many of us are now confined to a permanent amnesiac present, one throbbing with artificial life but unable to fathom where it came from or where it’s going.

Investigating The Time Warp

The collective sense that time is moving faster today than it has in the past has gained enough traction for scientists to start taking notice. A group of European psychologists has teamed up to form Time Experience in Europe’s Digital Age, abbreviated as TIMED. This research consortium, which includes some of the top time-perception researchers in Germany, Spain, Switzerland and the U.K., is using interviews, questionnaires and experiments to explore how our perception of time is influenced by how we use technology.

TIMED has spent the last three years collecting data from tens of thousands of study participants all over the world, and they’re now sharing the results of that project. In papers published so far, researchers have arrived at a number of important takeaways. First, people who spend more time on devices and social media platforms experience time passing more quickly. In one of their papers, Wittmann and his co-authors cited memory as a key factor in this correlation, with the use of digital technology limiting the breadth of people’s experiences and foreclosing on the events we most often remember.

“The collective sense that time is moving faster today than it has in the past has gained enough traction for scientists to start taking notice.”

“Routine activities such as repeatedly checking apps or prolonged online engagement for professional purposes could reduce the frequency of novel, embodied, and enactive experiences,” they wrote. “This, in turn, results in fewer rich or meaningful events being encoded in autobiographical memory. Consequently, such periods may retrospectively appear less eventful and more compressed, contributing to the feeling that time has passed quickly.”

Unsurprisingly, perhaps, researchers also found that excessive use of technological devices promoted a negative relationship with time. “Participants associated digital technology use with a loss of time, a desire to fill all time, a propensity to forget time and, as a result, a desire to gain greater control of time,” they wrote. Feeling that one’s relationship with time had spun out of control in turn spawned “feelings of guilt, shame, and a lack of self-control.”

Wittmann and his colleagues conducted qualitative interviews for TIMED, and some participants expressed frustration and even helplessness at how devices were transforming their sense of time. “What was really interesting to me was how people constantly talked about digital technology stealing their time,” Ruth Ogden, TIMED’s lead investigator, said. “One of the things that happens when you engage in doom scrolling and other forms of social media is you completely forget about time — time doesn’t exist anymore. So then you massively overextend how long you engage in these activities for.”

But Ogden doesn’t think that technology should be seen as the sole culprit for our warped perceptions of time. The strains in that relationship go deeper than memes, AI slop and infinite scroll, stemming from how modern society frames inert, unproductive states like boredom and “doing nothing.” In TIMED’s interviews, respondents also told Ogden and her colleagues they were uncomfortable with periods of inactivity and felt compelled to use their devices to fill every available gap in their schedule. “What we found through TIMED is that even when people have time, they don’t use it to do nothing,” she told me. “We live in a society that really values constantly being busy and constantly having something to do. We saw this in TIMED through people’s use of digital technology, where every bit of free time was spent on screens.”

If people were more comfortable with intervals that lacked so-called productivity — quiet longueurs, spells of boredom or periods of aimless reflection — they might stand a better chance of expanding and enriching the way they experience time. “It’s in those calm moments where we see a unique pattern of activity in the part of our brain responsible for helping to make our memories,” Hyman said. Those still, empty stretches are when we contemplate our immediate pasts, integrating them into the larger arc of our lives.

We know, however, that these states have been largely vaporized this decade — and only a seismic shift in our values and ideals stands a chance of reclaiming them. In Ogden’s eyes, the dilemma hinges on a simple question: “How do we get people back to being comfortable with doing very little and believing that doing little is not an indication of laziness?”

The Beauty Of Boredom

The stakes of this phenomenon can sometimes seem low. Feeling like time is speeding up is not a “kitchen table issue”; it won’t raise your taxes or make you go hungry. But the TIMED project has demonstrated that people who feel like they’re losing time are genuinely unhappy and even distressed about it. Members of Gen Z, in particular, don’t talk about the quickening pace of their lives with disinterested curiosity or frivolous bemusement — they lament it. When we lose our grip on the passage of time, it can feel like we’re also losing grip on our own lives.

Western culture views time as a currency to be leveraged, channeled and optimized. The societal pressure to perform productivity at all times is so insistent and thrumming that many of us — myself included — have lost the ability to slow down and luxuriate in the inherent slowness of time, the way it oozes forward like honey slithering across a glass jar. When Aldous Huxley was asked about time by an interlocutor in “The Doors of Perception,” his reply was both simple and profound. “There seems to be plenty of it,” he said. Untethered from his ego and all the worldly attachments it clung to, Huxley was able to tap into the spaciousness of existence — an amplitude and abundance that’s permanent and inviolable, if only we still had the freedom to see it.

“When we lose our grip on the passage of time, it can feel like we’re also losing grip on our own lives.”

It’s true that technology has capitalized on this culture of synchronized compliance. The companies that manufacture our devices and make the programs that run on them have wedged themselves into this perverse relationship to productivity, offering the badges and motifs that signify a certain enterprising competence. As Jenny Odell points out in her book, “How to Do Nothing,” there’s a battle playing out “for our time, a colonization of the self by capitalist ideas of productivity and efficiency.” Through these products, we personify the ideals of practicality and industriousness.

The pandemic, too, eventually fed into the hungry zeitgeist of maximizing our output and sacrificing ourselves on the altar of “getting ahead.” The increased use of communications platforms like Slack, Teams and Zoom promoted a porousness between our work and home lives, allowing what Odell calls a “certain nervous feeling, of being overstimulated and unable to sustain a train of thought” to infiltrate spaces long insulated from them.

This explains why many people feel that the way they experienced time during the pandemic never snapped back to how they processed it before Covid. In the aftermath, we became even more tethered to these platforms and other virtual spaces where productivity lingers at a low, insistent hum 24 hours a day. With our minds more anxious and overstimulated, our perception of time never had the chance to return to an earlier, more composed pace.

Further, trends that predated Covid resurfaced as though shot out of a cannon, and the ambient pressure to advance our lots at all costs imbued our culture with a mercenary quality. We were all racing to make more money, afford a home, secure a job, #YOLO at the live events we were unceremoniously robbed of. Amid this competitive turbulence — and the technologies that capitalized on our unease about it — everything started to move faster.

If we accept this premise, then maybe the crisis of time speeding up is not as hopelessly irreversible as it often seems. According to the latest time perception research, the amount of information our brains engage with shapes our subjective sense of how fast time is moving. If we intentionally reduce the stimuli we’re exposing ourselves to in a given day or week, then our brains will gradually slow down. And if our brains slow down, then our perception of time will taper off, too.

For their part, Ogden and other TIMED researchers feel that society has imposed too much responsibility on the individual to limit their use of technology. “Maybe it’s time that we shifted some of that onto the creators,” Ogden said. “The key metric for the success of digital technology is how long users are on it for, and how many people they can get on it for as long as possible. How do we flip that?” While we wait for those larger systemic changes, though, Ogden emphasized the importance of using our devices in a more intentional fashion. “What are you trying to get out of this digital technology use?” she asked. “You need to have an awareness of your own goals.”

In addition to modifying our own individual behavior, however, we also need to change the culture surrounding how we spend our time. That means coming to terms with the reality that boredom and “doing nothing” are neither shameful nor necessary evils. “There is huge value in doing nothing,” Ogden said. “We need to move away from thinking that it’s weird, lazy or slovenly.” Asked how she would spend a perfect holiday, Ogden described something very close to what people now labor so strenuously to avoid. “It would be to go and sit in a square in Italy with a nice glass of wine and watch the world go by.”

In his “Principles of Psychology,” William James invites us to participate in an experiment. “Close your eyes and simply wait to hear somebody tell you that a minute has elapsed,” he writes. The length of that single minute, he explains, will feel overwhelming. “You engulf yourself into its bowels as into those of that interminable first week of an ocean voyage, and find yourself wondering that history can have overcome many such periods in its course.” Those 60 seconds feel so full, James goes on, because “you attend so closely to the mere feeling of the time per se. ” When our senses are engaged and stimulated, time is compressed, disguised, eclipsed. “The feeling of bare time,” however, “is the least stimulating experience we can have.”

We used to tolerate those interminable minutes standing in a crowded grocery line, gazing out the convex glass window of an airplane, waiting for the dull red digits on an oven timer to run down to zero. These are now the endangered species of our day-to-day lives. And they are far more valuable than we ever could have known.
